messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 64
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Jeweler
- Trauma Type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
- Pcl5: 36

He grows up in a crowded Latin American household where silence is rare and fear is often louder than words. As a child, he learns early that his father’s anger can arrive without warning and that his mother’s body seems to anticipate it before anyone speaks. He remembers standing in a doorway as a small boy, too young to understand the full meaning of what he is seeing, watching his father shove his mother against furniture, hearing plates strike the floor, hearing his mother beg him to stop. The memories do not come to him as a neat sequence. They arrive in fragments: the smell of alcohol, the sound of footsteps in the hallway, the sight of his mother’s face afterward, swollen with shame and exhaustion. He says he learned to stay very still, to make himself small, because being unnoticed felt safer than being helpful.

As he gets older, he becomes alert to the mood of a room in a way other people do not seem to understand. He notices changes in tone, the tightening of a jaw, the quick movement of a hand. In school, he is quiet and watchful. At home, he becomes skilled at reading danger before it fully appears. He does not think of it as anxiety at the time; it feels more like common sense. When violence breaks out, he often hides nearby and listens. Afterward, he helps pick up what is broken. He learns to smooth things over, to act as if nothing happened. That habit of staying composed becomes a kind of survival skill, one he carries into adulthood.

As a young man, he leaves home determined to build a life that is orderly and controlled. He learns the craft of jewelry, drawn to the patience of it and the precision. In the workshop, he can spend hours at a bench shaping metal, setting stones, polishing a ring until it catches the light just right. The work suits him because it asks for focus and steadiness. He becomes known as careful, meticulous, someone who does not rush. He likes that the pieces are small enough to manage, that if something is bent or flawed, it can often be repaired. There is comfort in that. Unlike the chaos of childhood, the bench offers rules.

He marries, has children, and for a time builds the kind of life that looks stable from the outside. But he also carries a private vigilance that never fully lets up. Sudden shouting makes his chest tighten. Raised voices in a neighboring apartment or on the street can pull him back into himself without warning. He dislikes arguments and avoids them whenever possible. When his own marriage becomes strained years later, he finds himself shutting down rather than speaking. He can feel his body go rigid when conflict starts, and he often leaves the room or stays at work longer than necessary. His divorce is painful not only because of the loss, but because it confirms his belief that closeness eventually leads to hurt.

Now in his sixties, he lives alone and works less than he once did, though he still goes to the jewelry district most days because the routine helps him stay grounded. He says that if he skips too many days, his mind wanders into places he would rather not go. Certain sounds still startle him badly; a door slamming in the apartment building can make him flinch before he can stop himself. At night, he sometimes wakes with his heart racing after dreams he cannot fully remember, only the sense that he is back in the old house, hearing his mother cry. He does not often talk about those memories, but when he does, his voice becomes quieter and his gaze drifts away, as though he is watching something unfold at a distance.

He is deeply uncomfortable with scenes of family conflict on television and will change the channel without comment. He is also more irritable than he used to be, though he tries to hide it. He keeps to himself, has few close relationships, and admits that trust does not come easily. At the same time, he remains proud of the life he has made with his own hands. He notices beauty in detail, in a well-set stone or a finished clasp, and there is a steadiness in his work that feels like the opposite of the world he came from. Even now, he moves through life carefully, as if listening for something just beyond the next room.
